'''''Sisymbrium officinale''''', the '''hedge mustard''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> (formerly ''Erysimum officinale'') is a plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]].

==Description==
It is distinct from the [[mustard plant]]s which belong to the genus ''[[Brassica]]''. ''S. officinale'' is similar to other ''Sisymbrium'', but differs in its tall, erect stems with tiny flowers and fruits that are compacted parallel to the stem instead of hanging free.
''S.officinale'' grows to 80 cm high. The lower leaves are broad with two or three lateral lobes. The flowers are about 4 mm across and yellow. Fruits are long and without hairs when young but show hairs when mature and reach 18 mm long on [[Raceme|racemes]] pressed close to the stems.<ref>Parnell.J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press {{ISBN|978185918-4783}}</ref>

Hedge-mustard is food for the [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]], such as the [[Pieris rapae|small white]] (''[[Pieris rapae]]'').

==Distribution==
Once indigenous to North Africa and southern Europe,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sisymbrium officinale (common hedge-mustard): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/sisymbrium/officinale/ |access-date=2024-11-09 |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> but found in [[Ireland]],<ref>Scannell, M.P. and Synnott, D.M. 1972 ''A Census Catalogue of the Flora of Ireland'' Dublin Stationery Office</ref> [[Wales]] and [[England]] and also in the highlands of Scotland. <ref>Clapham, A.R,. Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 12968 ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles'' Cambridge University Press{{ISBN|0521046564}}</ref> It is found on roadsides, wasteland and as a weed of arable land.  It is now well-established throughout the world.

==Uses==
===In food===
This plant is widely cultivated across [[Europe]] for its edible leaves and seeds. It is widely used as a condiment in [[Northern Europe]] (particularly [[Denmark]], [[Norway]] and [[Germany]]).

The plant is also eaten in combination with [[yogurt]] in some parts of the [[Levant]].<ref>{{cite news |title="الحويرنة".. نبتة عشبية تتربع على موائد الأردنيين شتاء لتمدهم بالحيوية |url=https://alghad.com/story/784717 |access-date=30 October 2025 |work=[[Al Ghad]] |date=1 Feb 2020 |language=ar |trans-title="Al-Huwayrina"... a herbaceous plant that graces the tables of Jordanians in winter to provide them with vitality}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=ميرنا بامية لـ«الشرق الأوسط»: أبحث عن الأكلات التي توشك أن تسقط من الذاكرة |url=https://aawsat.com/home/article/1594566/%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%86%D8%A7-%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%84%D9%80%C2%AB%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%82-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%88%D8%B3%D8%B7%C2%BB-%D8%A3%D8%A8%D8%AD%D8%AB-%D8%B9%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%83%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AA%D9%8A-%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%B4%D9%83-%D8%A3%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%B3%D9%82%D8%B7-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B0%D8%A7%D9%83%D8%B1%D8%A9 |access-date=30 October 2025 |work=[[Asharq Al-Awsat]] |date=20 Feb 2019 |language=ar |trans-title=Mirna Bamiya told Asharq Al-Awsat: “I’m looking for dishes that are about to be forgotten.”}}</ref>

The leaves have a bitter [[cabbage]]-like flavour and they are used either in salads or cooked as a [[leaf vegetable]] (in cultivar versions). The [[seed]]s have been used to make [[Mustard (condiment)|mustard]] pastes in [[Europe]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sisymbrium+officinale |title=Plants for A Future Database - Sisymbrium officinale |accessdate=2007-05-25 |format= |work=Plants for a Future database }}</ref>

===Traditional medicine===
The Greeks believed it was an antidote to all poisons. In folk medicine, it was used to soothe sore throats - indeed one French name for it is the {{lang|fr|herbe aux chantres}} (the ''singers' plant''). This plant "grows by our roadsides and on waste ground, where it is a common weed, with a peculiar aptitude for collecting and retaining dust...it is named by the French the 'Singer's Plant,' it having been considered up to the time of Louis XIV an infallible remedy for loss of voice. Jean Racine, writing to Nicolas Boileau, recommends him to try the syrup...in order to be cured of voicelessness."<ref>M Greve & C F Leyel, ''A Modern Herbal,'' UK: Merchant Books, 1973, p.570</ref> It is "good for all diseases of the chest and lungs, hoarseness of voice...the juice...made into a syrup with honey or sugar, is no less effectual...for all other coughs, wheezing and shortness of breath...the seed is held to be a special remedy against poison and venom."<ref>N Culpeper, ''The Complete Herbal,'' UK: Wordsworth Editions, 1995, p.177</ref> It was "formerly used for hoarseness, weak lungs and to help the voice."<ref>R C Wren, ''Potter's New Cyclopedia of Botanical Drugs and Preparations,'' UK: C W Daniel Co, 1994, p.140</ref> Herbalists use the juice and flowers for [[bronchitis]] and [[stomach]] ailments, among other uses, and as a revitalizer.<ref>Howard, Michael. ''Traditional Folk Remedies'' (Century, 1987), p.153</ref> In [[Tibetan medicine]] it is used to repress the symptoms of food poisoning.<ref>[http://www2.bremen.de/info/nepal/Gallery-3/Medical/8-26/Medic26-7.htm#54 Medical Thangka]</ref>
